name: sonnet-criteria-llama31-8b/13
question: I just received a $10,000 tax refund. What's the smartest thing to do with it?
criteria: immediate guaranteed return on debt payoff
plausible_answers: Answer A (Debt and Invest Default): Pay off any high-interest debt first, top up your emergency fund to 3 months, then invest the remainder as a lump sum in a broad index fund — this order maximizes guaranteed and expected returns.

Answer B (Lump Sum Invest): If you have no high-interest debt and a full emergency fund, invest the entire $10k immediately as a lump sum — two-thirds of the time this beats spreading contributions and markets reward early investment.

Answer C (DCA Over 6 Months): Spread the $10k across 6 monthly investments to reduce the risk of deploying at a market peak — you sacrifice some expected return but avoid the regret of an immediate post-investment downturn.
sources:
Source 1 (2023, NerdWallet, USA): The standard priority order: pay off high-interest debt first, then build or top up your emergency fund, then maximize tax-advantaged retirement contributions, then invest in a taxable brokerage.

Source 2 (2022, Investopedia, USA): A lump sum invested immediately in a broad market index fund outperforms dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time historically, because markets trend upward — but DCA reduces regret risk if markets fall soon after investing.

Source 3 (2023, Reddit r/personalfinance, USA): Community advice: resist lifestyle inflation, don't keep it in a checking account, and follow the personal finance flowchart — high-interest debt → emergency fund → IRA → 401k → taxable brokerage.

Source 4 (2022, Morningstar, USA): Lump-sum investing a windfall into a diversified portfolio has historically been the mathematically superior approach, but investors who lump-sum at a market peak and panic-sell underperform those who spread contributions over 3–6 months.

Source 5 (2021, WSJ, USA): Using a windfall to eliminate high-interest consumer debt provides a guaranteed risk-free return equal to the interest rate — for debt above 7–8%, this often beats expected market returns on a risk-adjusted basis.
